lead: A scene graph is a tree that stores a virtual world as nodes. Each node holds a transform, geometry, material, camera or light. A toolkit walks the tree, combines parent and child transforms, and draws only what the current camera can see. The idea exists because a flat list of objects makes transforms, state changes and culling hard to manage. It is used in VR engines, AR SDKs, simulators and 3D modelling tools. The tree gives one clear order for updates, drawing and collision checks.
prereq: You need: object hierarchies and transformation matrices from Unit 4, Kinematics modeling, plus basic vectors and coordinates.

sections.h3: Scene graph as a retained tree

blocks.text: A scene graph is a retained-mode description of a world. The application builds nodes once, keeps them, and the toolkit redraws the world from those nodes every frame. A node is a record. It may be a group, a transform, a geometry mesh, a material, a camera or a light. Group and transform nodes have children; leaf nodes hold drawable data or view data.

items: Group node: orders children and applies no geometry itself.
Transform node: stores translation, rotation and scale for its subtree.
Geometry node: stores vertices and faces; material node stores colour, texture and shader state.
Camera and light nodes: define view and illumination.

blocks.text: The toolkit traverses depth first. It pushes a parent transform, composes it with the child transform, reaches a geometry node, sets its material and draws it. The same order fixes state changes: if node A sets a red material and node B does not set a material, B may inherit red. Toolkits save and restore state or use state sorting to avoid this leak. Each node can also carry a bounding volume, a simple box or sphere around its contents. A camera frustum test rejects whole subtrees, so culling is cheap.

Local coordinates are measured in a node's own frame. World coordinates are measured in the scene frame. A point p local in node M becomes world by applying every transform from the root down to M, in that order.

blocks.where: p_world is the point in world coordinates; p_local is the point in M's local frame; T_T is the transform of T, M's parent; T_M is the transform of M.

items: Start with the scene root. Here the root is identity, so its frame is the world frame.
Apply T's translation of +2 m on x: T's origin is at world x = 2 m.
Apply M's translation of +3 m on x: M's origin is at world x = 2 + 3 = 5 m.
Add the point's local x = 1 m: world x = 5 + 1 = 6 m.

blocks.text: For pure translations the numbers add, so this example checks frame order, not arithmetic order. With rotation or non-uniform scale, matrix order changes the result.

Unity uses a scene made of GameObjects. A GameObject has a Transform and components. Components attach geometry, materials, cameras, lights and scripts. A prefab is a reusable saved GameObject subtree. Instantiating a prefab copies the tree and keeps links to the asset. Unity and Unreal are engines in Chapter 5.5.

Unreal Engine uses a level made of Actors. An Actor is an object with a transform and components. A level is the scene graph; Blueprints and C++ classes define behaviour. Scripts attach behaviour, covered in Chapter 5.6.

OpenSceneGraph is a C++ toolkit built directly around a scene graph. Nodes include group, transform, geode and state set. It is used in simulators and visualisation where a program needs explicit control of traversal and culling.

VRML and X3D are file formats that describe a scene graph for web or interchange. A VRML or X3D file stores nodes for transforms, shapes, materials, lights and viewpoints. Most courses teach the same tree idea through an engine rather than through X3D. AR SDKs such as ARCore, ARKit and Vuforia also keep a retained graph of trackables, anchors and models. Their tracking and display details are in Unit 6.

spec.aria: A tree with root S, children T and Camera, T's child M and M's point P; beside it a world x axis with hops of 2, 3 and 1 metres landing P at 6.

examples.question: A scene graph has root S. S has child T with translation +2 m on x and child Camera. T has child M with translation +3 m on x. M has a point P at local coordinates (1, 0, 0) m. The scene root has identity transform. Compute the world x coordinate of P.
steps: Root S is identity, so its frame is the world frame.
T translates +2 m on x relative to S. T's origin is at world x = 2 m.
M translates +3 m on x relative to T. M's origin is at world x = 2 + 3 = 5 m.
P has local x = 1 m in M. World x = 5 + 1 = 6 m.
examples.answer: The world x coordinate of P is 6 m.

traps: Parent transform applies before child transform. Write T_T × T_M × p_local, not T_M × T_T × p_local.
Local coordinates belong to the node's own frame; world coordinates belong to the scene root. Do not mix them in one vector.
A scene graph is not the rendering pipeline. The graph stores the world; the pipeline turns triangles into pixels.
Inherited state can leak between siblings. A material set in one branch may affect a later sibling unless the toolkit saves and restores state.
A bounding volume must enclose the real geometry. A box that is too small culls visible objects; a box that is too large wastes draw calls.

quiz.a: A tree of nodes that stores a virtual world, with transforms, geometry, materials, cameras and lights, so a toolkit can traverse and draw it.

quiz.q: Name four node types found in a scene graph.
quiz.a: Any four of: group, transform, geometry, material, camera, light.

quiz.q: Why does a toolkit traverse a scene graph depth first?
quiz.a: Depth-first traversal carries the parent transform down to each child. A child cannot get its world transform until its parent's transform is known.
The application keeps a scene description between frames. The toolkit redraws from that retained description instead of the application resending every object each frame.

quiz.q: T translates +4 m on x. M is a child of T and translates -1 m on x. A point is at local x = 2 m in M. What is its world x?
quiz.a: M's origin is at 4 - 1 = 3 m. The point is at 3 + 2 = 5 m.

quiz.q: A parent has scale 2 on x and origin at world x = 0. A child has local translation +3 m on x. The parent transform applies first. What is the child origin's world x?
quiz.a: Apply parent scale to the child translation: 2 × 3 = 6 m. The world x is 6 m.

quiz.q: A scene has 1000 leaf nodes. Explain how bounding volumes reduce draw calls.
quiz.a: Each subtree gets a simple box or sphere. The toolkit tests that volume against the camera frustum. If it is outside, the whole subtree is skipped, so many leaves are rejected with one test.

quiz.q: Why can state leakage cause wrong colours during scene graph traversal?
quiz.a: A material set in one branch may remain active when a sibling is drawn. If the sibling does not set its own material, it inherits the earlier one. Saving and restoring state, or sorting by state, prevents this.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern interchange formats such as glTF and Universal Scene Description carry scene-graph structure across tools. WebXR applications build a scene graph in JavaScript and submit it to the headset each frame. Researchers also use scene graphs for semantic understanding, where nodes carry labels for AR. Search for glTF node hierarchy, USD composition arcs, and WebXR scene graph.
